---
title: "Repeated units in linguistic data"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

Recall the distinction between a **recorded observation** and an **independent sampling unit**. The discussion of [independent sampling](../statistical-inference/independent-sampling.qmd) used the first term for a value written in the data table and the second for a unit that contributes a new draw under the sampling model. These counts agree in a simple random sample with one observation per unit. They come apart in many linguistic experiments because one participant supplies several responses and one item receives responses from several participants.

A [residual](residuals.qmd) is observed minus fitted response. Repetition matters because rows sharing a participant or spoken word may have related residuals even after the mean predictors are supplied.

Here is the basic problem in three observed MALD trials. The first two rows below come from one listener. The first and third contain the same spoken word but come from different listeners.

```{r}
#| label: mald-three-repeated-unit-rows
mald_preview <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
item_participant_counts <- tapply(
  mald_preview$participant_id,
  mald_preview$item,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
)
preview_item <- names(item_participant_counts)[
  item_participant_counts > 1L
][[1L]]
item_rows <- mald_preview[mald_preview$item == preview_item, ]
preview_participant <- item_rows$participant_id[[1L]]
first_row <- item_rows[1L, ]
participant_row <- mald_preview[
  mald_preview$participant_id == preview_participant &
    mald_preview$item != preview_item,
][1L, ]
item_row <- item_rows[
  item_rows$participant_id != preview_participant,
][1L, ]
repetition_example <- rbind(first_row, participant_row, item_row)
repetition_example[c("participant_id", "item", "rt_ms", "correct")]
```

There are three response rows, but the observations reuse two of their sources. Rows 1 and 2 may resemble one another because one listener supplied both responses; rows 1 and 3 may resemble one another because both contain `r preview_item`. A row count alone cannot tell us how many distinct sources of information the table contains. We need the participant and item identifiers as well.

We examine that structure in a connected set of MALD trials. MALD is an auditory lexical decision database described by Tucker et al. ([2019](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1)); the later [MALD version 1.1](https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116) expanded the participant inventory. The paper reports 231 listeners, whereas version 1.1 contains 440. These totals describe different versions and should not be combined.

## Examining repetition in the MALD table

The extract used here contains a connected set of participants and words selected without consulting correctness or response time. One row records one real-word trial from one participant, including the spoken word, response time, correctness, SUBTLEX frequency, acoustic duration, and position within the experimental run.

```{r}
#| label: mald-structure
mald_all <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald_all, correct == 1L)

participant_counts <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id,
  data = mald,
  FUN = length
)
item_counts <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ item,
  data = mald,
  FUN = length
)

structure_summary <- c(
  connected_rows = nrow(mald_all),
  correct_latency_rows = nrow(mald),
  participants = length(unique(mald$participant_id)),
  word_items = length(unique(mald$item)),
  participant_word_pairs = nrow(unique(mald[c("participant_id", "item")]))
)
structure_summary
```

The first retained source row makes these fields concrete:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-mald-trial
mald_all[1L, c(
  "participant_id", "session_id", "run_id", "trial_order", "item",
  "rt_ms", "correct", "frequency_subtlex", "duration_ms", "n_phones",
  "n_syllables"
)]
```

`participant_id` names the listener; `run_id` names that listener's run; `trial_order` locates the trial within the run; `item` is the spoken word; `rt_ms` is onset-to-response time; and `correct` records the lexical decision's accuracy. Frequency, acoustic duration, phone count, and syllable count belong to the word and thus repeat whenever that word is presented. Participant and word identifiers determined the connected subset before we examined response time or correctness. We imposed the correct response restriction later when defining the latency analysis.

The latency analysis retains correct responses, as in Tucker et al.'s source analysis. This restriction leaves `r format(nrow(mald), big.mark = ",")` trials from `r length(unique(mald$participant_id))` participants and `r format(length(unique(mald$item)), big.mark = ",")` spoken words. It does not make the retained rows independent.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-repetition
library(ggplot2)

repetition_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    unit = "Participant",
    repetitions = participant_counts$log_rt
  ),
  data.frame(
    unit = "Word item",
    repetitions = item_counts$log_rt
  )
)

ggplot(repetition_data, aes(x = repetitions)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey55", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~unit, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Correct trials per unit", y = "Units") +
  theme_classic()
```

The two panels show different replication structures. A participant contributes many lexical decisions, while a word is heard by more than one participant. Thus the trial count, participant count, and item count answer different questions.

## Writing the independence claim

A regression model without grouping terms often represents conditional independence as

$$
f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_i f(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

After the predictors are known, the joint density is written as a product over trials. Under this model, learning the residual for one row gives no information about the residual for another.

That claim is implausible here for two distinct reasons. Responses from one participant may resemble each other because that listener has a persistent response-speed baseline. Responses to one word may resemble each other because its acoustic and lexical properties are not completely represented by the measured predictors. Observing one trial can thus change what we expect for another trial that shares its participant or word.

## Distinguishing crossed and nested units

We call participant and word **crossed units** because participants respond to many words and words receive responses from multiple participants. By contrast, we call one unit [**nested**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=261) within another when each lower-level unit belongs to only one higher-level unit. For instance, each MALD run belongs to one participant session; a run identifier does not migrate between participants. These names describe the incidence pattern in the table, not the order of its columns.

The distinction can be checked from the incidence table rather than inferred from column order:

```{r}
#| label: mald-crossing-check
crossing_check <- c(
  smallest_participant_item_inventory = min(participant_counts$log_rt),
  largest_participant_item_inventory = max(participant_counts$log_rt),
  smallest_item_listener_inventory = min(item_counts$log_rt),
  largest_item_listener_inventory = max(item_counts$log_rt)
)
crossing_check
```

For intuition, the following small incidence table marks whether each of the first five participants contributed a retained correct response to each of the first eight displayed words:

```{r}
#| label: show-mald-incidence-example
example_participants <- unique(mald$participant_id)[seq_len(5L)]
example_items <- unique(mald$item)[seq_len(8L)]
xtabs(
  ~ participant_id + item,
  data = subset(
    mald,
    participant_id %in% example_participants & item %in% example_items
  )
)
```

Rows and columns both contain multiple marks. That pattern is crossing. A nested design would place every lower-level unit in exactly one higher-level row or column.

## Matching dependence to the claim

A claim that extends across listeners requires replication across participants. A claim that extends across lexical items requires replication across words. A claim about both requires a design and analysis that preserve both sources. More trials from the same participants or words can improve estimates for those particular units, but those trials do not introduce new participants or words.

Averaging trials within participants would preserve participant replication while discarding word variation and predictors that change across a participant's trials. Averaging within words would do the reverse. Mixed effects models retain responses at the trial level while representing both shared sources.

Before fitting one, record four facts: (i) what one response row represents, (ii) which sampled units recur, (iii) whether those units are crossed or nested, and (iv) the populations across which the linguistic association should generalize. We can then translate those design facts into [population coefficients and group distributions](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd).

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why are two trials from one listener not independent merely because they have different row numbers?
2. Why are participant and word crossed rather than nested?
3. What changes if trials are averaged within words?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The trials may share a persistent listener baseline and other unmeasured listener properties. A model must assert conditional independence; different spreadsheet rows do not establish it. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. Participants respond to multiple words, and words receive responses from multiple participants. Neither unit belongs to only one level of the other. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. Word averaging preserves word replication but removes participant identities, participant variation, and predictors that change within participants. The estimand then concerns items. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

The next step is to represent this dependence inventory with [population coefficients and group deviations](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd).
